backups.note: What happens to backups over time, and how the space they take is counted (issue #242). DECIDED by Russell, 2026-09-21 (option C): keep every backup a teacher makes, and make the space they take VISIBLE - per course and in total - with a way to delete several at once. The assistant's own backups keep their cap. AUTHORED; edit as text. pruneCases run the pruning that follows a new backup, sizeCases the count, deleteCases the delete. Formatting a byte count is each platform's own ('105.6 MB' on the mac, the way Finder writes it), so the cases carry bytes only.
backups.assistantKeptWhy: The assistant saves one backup per conversation whether or not anybody asked, so it clears up after itself: the five most recent of ITS backups of a course are kept, counted per course, and a backup whose stamp cannot be true is neither counted nor deleted (zipNames.couldHaveBeenStamped).
backups.teacherBackupsPrunedWhy: A backup made on purpose before a risky change should not vanish because ten more were made after it - deciding on a teacher's behalf that last month's copy has expired is not the app's call. The fault was never that they are kept but that nothing SHOWED the space, so the space is shown and deleting old ones is made easy; the teacher decides what goes. A cap for teacher backups with the oldest shown before removal was the alternative considered and not chosen.
backups.mediaIsAlwaysIncludedWhy: Every backup carries the whole course, Media included - measured at 467 MB and 9.7 s for a real course with 487 MB of Media. REJECTED, and recorded so it is not proposed again: a lighter backup that leaves Media out. Restoring one would DELETE the course's Media.
backups.sizeIsLogicalWhy: The size shown is the file's LOGICAL size (on the mac, fileSize), never what it occupies on this disk. A working folder kept in iCloud Drive can have its backups evicted to the cloud, where they take almost nothing on this disk while costing their whole size in the teacher's cloud storage - and costing it on this disk again the moment one is restored. Measured on the sparse shape of an evicted file: logical 244.84 GB, on disk 'Zero KB'. The on-disk number would tell that teacher their backups take nothing. Not measured on a real evicted file, and whether a deleted file keeps costing cloud storage while in that service's own recently-deleted folder is not measured either - so nothing promises the space is freed at once.
backups.neverDeletedWhileAConversationCanRestore: An open assistant conversation offers 'Restore Section N...' from the backup it made before its first change. Deleting that backup - one click after selecting the assistant's backups, which is exactly what the #242 plan review reasoned from the code - leaves a button that fails after the teacher has agreed to it. So a delete leaves it alone, deletes everything else asked for, and says which assistant window to close (the same 'Close the assistant for <course> Section <n> first' a second assistant window is refused with).

pruneCases.name: the assistant keeps its five most recent, and none of the teacher's is touched
pruneCases.why: Seven assistant backups and three of the teacher's: the two OLDEST assistant backups go. The teacher's three are not counted among the five and are not deleted, however old.

pruneCases.name: a teacher's own backups are never pruned, however many there are
pruneCases.why: Twelve of the teacher's own backups and none of the assistant's: nothing is deleted. Russell's decision on #242.

pruneCases.name: an archive and the setup wizard's zip are never pruned
pruneCases.why: Six assistant backups beside an archive and the wizard's automatic zip: only the oldest assistant backup goes. The other two share the folder but are not backups at all.

sizeCases.name: backups are counted per course and in total; archives and the wizard's zips are not
sizeCases.why: The shape of Russell's real folder early in a term: teacher and assistant backups of two courses, beside an archive and a setup-wizard zip that are not in the Backups list and so are not in its total - a number the teacher cannot act on from that list would only mislead. Courses are listed in course-code order.

sizeCases.name: the logical size counts, not what the file takes on this disk
sizeCases.why: A file whose contents are not on this disk - the shape of one a cloud service has evicted - still counts at its whole size, which is what it costs in the teacher's cloud storage and what it will take again when restored. A runner makes it sparse (the mac truncates an empty file to the size) so the case costs no disk; counted by what the disk holds it would be nearly nothing.

deleteCases.name: several backups are deleted at once, and only those
deleteCases.why: Three of five, permanently - as the single delete always was and as its confirmation says.

deleteCases.name: the backup an open assistant conversation can restore from is kept, and the rest are deleted
deleteCases.why: The assistant window for Section 2 is open and made this backup before its first change; its Restore button puts the section back from it. It is kept and the teacher is told which window to close. The other backup asked for is still deleted - one refusal is not a reason to stop.

deleteCases.name: an older assistant backup is not held just because the assistant is open
deleteCases.why: Only the backups the OPEN conversation made are held. An assistant backup from an earlier conversation about the same section is an ordinary backup now, and a rule keyed on 'made by the assistant' or 'this section' would refuse it for nothing.

normalized.why: Trimmed and upper-cased before anything else looks at it. A Mac's disk is case-insensitive but case-preserving, so ICS3U and ics3u cannot both exist as folders — settling the case here is what stops a clash check missing one.

courseCode.note: What a course code may be — letters, numbers, dashes, and single spaces between them, at most twelve characters. ONE rule, asked by the New Course wizard and by renaming a course, because a code one accepts and the other refuses is a course a teacher can create and then never re-type. The rule is narrow because a course code is not just a label: it IS the folder name under courses/, it is written into course_config.json for the shared Python, it prefixes every backup and archive zip, and on the mac it becomes part of a scheduled publish's launchd label. Each of those has its own opinion about what it will carry; one narrow rule beats four that disagree at the edges.

clubDetection.note: Whether a course code names a CLUB rather than a course. It decides two things a teacher can see: whether the New Course wizard offers a "Short label" field, and whether custom_short_name is written into course_config.json. Ask the course-name CATALOG first and take its answer as final — a code the app ships a name for is a course, whatever shape it happens to be. Only for a code the catalog has never heard of does the fallback apply: four characters or more, and the fourth is not a digit. That fallback is an Ontario-shaped guess (ICS3U, MPM2D put the grade digit fourth) and it is kept only for teacher-invented names like CODING or ROBOTICS, where there is no entry to consult.
clubDetection.why: Added 2026-08-23 after the fallback was found running on its own on BOTH platforms. British Columbia's codes put a letter or a dash in fourth place — MTEL-12, MMA--09, MCMPR11 — so every one of BC's 117 courses was read as a club, and a real course was offered a club's short-label field. macOS fixed it in ClubCodeRule; NewCourseDialog.IsClubCode on Windows still carries the original one-line version, so this case list is expected to fail there until it does. That is the contract working, not damage.

cases.why: An Ontario course: the catalog knows it, and the fallback would agree anyway.

courseCode.wordingNote: Every problem has TWO wordings and both are teacher-facing. expectProblem is the full sentence, shown under the New Course wizard's wide field where it can afford to explain itself. expectShort is what the SIDEBAR row shows while a course is being renamed in place, where there is room for about twenty-five characters before the message is cut off mid-word — and half an explanation explains nothing. Both come off one enum in the code, so they cannot drift into two different rules.

problems.why: An empty field is not-ready-yet, not an error. A warning that appears before the teacher has typed anything is noise.
A single space BETWEEN letters or numbers is allowed — teachers really do name a course “AP CALC”. Everything downstream already copes with one; the launchd label sanitiser exists precisely for it.

problems.expectProblem: A course code can’t have two spaces in a row.
problems.why: Two in a row is a typo every time, and it is checked before the character rule so the commonest mistake gets the sentence that names it.
Leading and trailing spaces are TRIMMED rather than refused — the stored code never carries one, and refusing a teacher for a space they did not mean to type helps nobody.
Nothing but spaces trims to nothing, which is not-ready-yet rather than an error.

problems.expectProblem: A course named ICS4U already exists. If that's last year's, keep a copy of it for reference and then remove it.
problems.why: The clash is found case-insensitively — see normalized.

problems.expectProblem: A course named MPM2D already exists. If that's last year's, keep a copy of it for reference and then remove it.
A course code can only use letters, numbers, spaces and dashes.

problems.why: A hyphen is ALLOWED, reversed 2026-08-23. This case used to expect a refusal, on the reasoning that a hyphen is punctuation like any other and CS CLUB with a space is the way to write a club. That reasoning was written before British Columbia's codes were in the app: 55 of the 117 codes in support/british_columbia_secondary_courses.json contain a dash — MTEL-12, MFMP-10, MMA--09 — so the rule was refusing more than half of one province's real courses. A dash is safe everywhere a code travels: legal in a folder name, in a zip's name, and in a launchd label.
A real BC course code, and the one Russell was trying to create when he found the rule refusing it.
Two dashes in a row are fine — the double-character check is about SPACES, where a run is always a typo. A run of dashes is what BC actually prints for its shorter subject codes.

A leading or trailing dash is not refused. Unlike a space, it is not trimmed either, so the code is stored with it — allowed rather than special-cased, because nothing downstream minds and a rule with fewer edges is a rule both apps can hold.

problems.expectProblem: A course code can only use letters, numbers, spaces and dashes.
problems.why: Emoji fail the same test punctuation does: not an ASCII letter or digit.

problems.expectProblem: A course code can only use letters, numbers, spaces and dashes.
problems.why: An accented letter is refused too. The sentence says letters and numbers, which is true of what is ALLOWED — the alternative is a sentence about character encodings in a sidebar row.
Ontario codes are six; clubs and locally-named courses are named by the teacher.
Ten characters including a space — the shape twelve was chosen to allow.

problems.expectProblem: A course code can be at most 12 characters.
problems.why: Thirteen. The limit counts the space.
A course does not clash with itself. Re-typing a course's own code while renaming it is a teacher changing their mind, which is allowed.
Nor does it clash with its own capitalisation.

problems.expectProblem: A course named MPM2D already exists. If that's last year's, keep a copy of it for reference and then remove it.
problems.why: Renaming onto ANOTHER course's code is still a clash.

renameEffects.why: The code IS the folder name under courses/, so renaming is a move. Everything inside the folder travels with it untouched.

The app reads a course's code from its FOLDER name while the site builder and the social-card maker read it from course_config.json. A pair that disagree produce a sidebar saying one thing and a published page saying another, with no error anywhere.
course_name is the teacher's own wording and is editable in Course Settings. Rewriting a title they may have hand-written, because they changed a code, is the kind of helpfulness that loses work.

They stay in courses/_backups/<OLD CODE>/ under the names they were made with, because that is what they are: a copy of the course as it stood, when it was called that. Restoring one still works — the restorer names the restored folder after the ITEM rather than after whatever the zip holds inside.

Where a section publishes to is recorded INSIDE the course folder (.netlify_sites/section<N>.json), so it moves with it and the site's address does not change. A rename is a change to the teacher's filing, not a move of their students' URL.

The one thing renaming has to break. A scheduled publish is an alarm held OUTSIDE the working folder, addressed by the old code, and after a rename it would fire at a course that is no longer there. It is turned off and the teacher is told — silently losing a scheduled publish is the failure worth spending an alert on.

cases.why: Trimmed and upper-cased before the lookup, exactly as the code field itself is.
British Columbia course code lookup.
British Columbia course code lookup.
British Columbia course code lookup.
A club code is in no lookup, so nothing is filled in and the teacher types their own name.

defaultCourseName.note: The course name a NEW course starts with, filled in from the code. It is the SHORT name from the regional course registries (support/*_secondary_courses.json), not the formal one. The formal name is the ministry's string — "Introduction to Computer Science, Grade 11, U" — which is correct and which almost nobody wants as a website title: defaulting to it only means the teacher deletes it before typing what they actually call the course. Both names stay one button away in the wizard, and the command-line wizard offers them in the same order (short first, then formal, then a custom name). The fill only ever replaces an empty field or a previous fill of its own, so a teacher's own typing is never overwritten.

cases.why: BC trailing 2-digit grade 11.
BC trailing 2-digit grade 10.
BC trailing 2-digit grade 09.
No digit in the fourth place or recognized trailing grade, so no grade is claimed.
Too short to have a fourth character.
A digit that is not 1–4 is honest about not knowing rather than silently dropping it.

gradeLabels.note: The grade named by a course code across supported jurisdictions (Ontario 4th character digit, BC trailing 2-digit grade), matching the wizard. A club code with no recognized grade gets no grade label at all rather than a wrong one.

note: Names on disk and the rules for adding a section. All of it is string handling over files both apps read, so all of it ports — and the naming grammar in particular MUST, because the two apps list each other's files. A course backed up on a Mac and opened on Windows has to appear in the Backups list, not vanish because the parser was rewritten from memory.

cases.shape: the setting for section 1 on the line BELOW its key, hidden: the pair goes after the whole value, and is held back because a value that runs onto the next line is not copied (measured: put between the key and its value, as before the review of #175, section 1 read no setting and was PUBLISHED, and section 2 read 'false false', also published)

addingKeysToAPage.measured: GitHub #175, 2026-09-25, each of the first five `before`s run through the build's own process_frontmatter for section 2 (python-frontmatter 1.3.0, PyYAML 6.0.3): every one comes out with NO publish key — shown to students — and every `after` comes out with section 1's value, so the two pages hidden in section 1 stay hidden. Before the fix the mac skipped every shape but the first (the page left unchanged). Pointing the finder at the shared rule while keeping the old character-count splice was measured too: the three shapes whose fence is not exactly `---` on the first line got a new date ending in a stray character of the old text (`…-0400e`), and the Windows-line-ending page lost its frontmatter entirely — the build read no keys and printed the block as the page's first lines.
addingKeysToAPage.rule: Adding a section gives every course-level page that carries per-section keys a `createdSection<N>` (the given date) and a `publishForSection<N>` copied from the LOWEST existing section, as two new lines straight after the last per-section key and its whole value (any lines it continues onto). The copy is written HELD BACK (`false`) instead when the lowest section's setting cannot be read as one value: its value runs onto the next line, it is not complete on its own line, or it is a legacy `draftSection<N>` value the reader cannot tell - the safe direction, counted on the trail's `section added` line. The frontmatter is found the way the build finds it — a fence of three dashes or more, blank lines allowed before it, spaces after it — and the page is changed ONLY by inserting those lines: the teacher's fence, anything before it, the body and the line endings (a new line takes the ending of the line it follows) stay byte for byte. A page with no per-section keys is left alone.
addingKeysToAPage.why: A page the finder missed got no key for the new section, and a page with no key is SHOWN — so a page the teacher had hidden in section 1 was published in the new section, and nothing said so. The issue's first reading, that a missed page 'falls back to its plain publish: value', is wrong for the ordinary course-level page, which has no plain key. Whole-file equality is the test because a check for the new key's presence passes the wrong splice.

What a Buddhist-calendar machine wrote before the mac pinned its formatter. Read as Gregorian it is the year 2569, five centuries from now.

An ETHIOPIC machine, and the case the bounds exist for: read as Gregorian it is an ordinary date in the past that a person would not blink at. Only 'before Plantoir could have written one' separates it, which is why the floor is a date in this product's own history rather than a round number.

couldHaveBeenStamped.note: Whether a moment is one Plantoir could have stamped into a zip's name. Shared because it is the rule that decides what gets DELETED: PruneBackups (CourseArchiver on both sides) sorts the assistant's backups by the date in their NAME and throws the tail away, so a name written in another machine's calendar — 2569, on a folder carried from a pre-fix Mac — parses cleanly, sorts as the newest thing in the folder, takes one of the five kept places and pushes a real backup off the disk. A stamp this refuses must be neither counted nor deleted; it is still LISTED, so the teacher can restore or delete it themselves. The floor is 2025-01-01 because the archive feature was written on 2026-08-09 and nothing of this kind can be older: set a year and a half earlier it refuses no real name, and it still clears the nearest wrong reading (Ethiopic, 7 years 8 months behind) by six years. ASCII digits and a Gregorian reading throughout, so this list runs identically under en_US_POSIX and CultureInfo.InvariantCulture — unlike the mac's own migration for the old spellings, which is deliberately NOT shared. Proposed from the mac 2026-09-10 (issue #160); Windows deserialises zipNames by key name, so an unknown block leaves its suite GREEN until it is wired up, and issue #161 asks for that. The guard itself is already there: #161's first half landed on 2026-09-19, with these same two bounds held by a test of its own until this list replaces it.

moment.format: yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss, in the LOCAL time zone
moment.note: The moment a recognised name is read as. Pinned because the stamp is written and read in the GREGORIAN calendar on every machine, whatever calendar the machine itself is set to. A date formatter given no locale renders `yyyy` in the CURRENT LOCALE'S calendar, so the same instant is spelled `2569-08-09_141530` on a Buddhist-calendar machine, `0008-08-09_141530` on a Japanese one and `1448-02-26_141530` on an Islamic one (measured on macOS 26 for 2026-08-09 14:15:30) — none of them a name this file says Plantoir writes, and none of them sortable once the folder is opened anywhere else. Windows has always pinned `CultureInfo.InvariantCulture`; the mac pinned `en_US_POSIX` on 2026-09-10 for issue #160, and also goes on READING the old spellings, because a teacher on such a machine has zips already named that way and refusing them would empty their Archives and Backups lists on the day they updated. That reading half is the mac's own migration and is deliberately not a case here: the mac cannot check it on the other side, because .NET's TryParseExact does not treat native digits the way Foundation does. Issue #161 carries what Windows was asked to do about it. The live defect it named — a backup named in another machine's calendar sorts as the newest thing in the folder, and their PruneBackups had no guard against a date that cannot be true — was fixed there on 2026-09-19; what is still owed is asserting these values.

zipNames.note: Three kinds of zip live side by side in `courses/_backups/<CODE>/`, told apart by NAME. Each parser accepts only its own form, so the three can never appear in each other's lists — an archive showing up under Backups is a teacher restoring the wrong thing. The timestamp is `yyyy-MM-dd_HHmmss` and contains an underscore of its own, which is why the pieces are counted rather than split on the last underscore.
